Cases, readings, and evidence
The main textbook is Anderson et al. (2020), 8th edition. Selected Chapter 7 material develops sampling and sampling distributions; selected Chapter 8 material develops mean and proportion intervals and planning.

EAI employees: population summaries p.308; sample summaries p.316; finite correction and CLT pp.323–324.
Lloyd’s spending: known-SD inputs p.357.
Household credit-card balances: rounded sample summaries and t interval pp.367–368.
Women golfers: survey counts and normal interval p.378; planning pp.380–381.

We use stated book parameters and summaries rather than introducing unverified observation files. Artificial simulations and original planning extensions are labeled. No new workbook-to-CSV match is claimed.

title: Module 4: Proportions and Sample-size Planning
section: Business case: women golfers and tee times
text:
Business case: women golfers and tee times
The textbook reports a national survey of 900 women golfers, of whom 396 were satisfied with the availability of tee times. What interval estimates the population proportion satisfied? How many completed responses would a new survey need for a margin of error of 0.025 at 95% confidence? We use the published counts and planning question, not verified individual responses or an independently checked survey design.

يعرض الكتاب مسحًا وطنيًا شمل 900 لاعبة غولف، كانت 396 منهن راضيات عن توافر مواعيد بدء اللعب. ما الفترة التي تقدّر نسبة الراضيات في المجتمع؟ وكم استجابة مكتملة يحتاجها مسح جديد لهامش خطأ 0.025 عند مستوى ثقة 95%؟ نستخدم الأعداد وسؤال التخطيط المنشورين، وليس استجابات فردية جرى التحقق منها أو تصميم مسح تحقّقنا منه بصورة مستقلة.

title: Module 4: Proportions and Sample-size Planning
section: From a binary response to a proportion
text:
From a binary response to a proportion
Define success before counting: here it means satisfied, not every favorable response on an unspecified question. For \(x\) successes among \(n\) responses,
\[\hat p=\frac{x}{n},\qquad \widehat{SE}=\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}.\]
\[
\hat p\ \pm\ z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat{SE}.\]
This is the normal or Wald interval. It assumes a design supporting independent binary responses or an appropriate small sampling fraction, and a meaningful target population. Check \(n\hat p\geq10\) and \(n(1-\hat p)\geq10\) in this course. A large count does not establish representative selection or eliminate nonresponse bias.

# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# The success denominator includes all 900 surveyed women golfers, not only the satisfied respondents.
# qnorm(.975) is the two-sided 95% normal critical value; sqrt() computes the estimated SE.
x <- 396
n <- 900
phat <- x/n
se <- sqrt(phat*(1-phat)/n)
margin <- qnorm(.975)*se
ci <- phat+c(-1,1)*margin
knitr::kable(data.frame(Estimate=phat, Successes=x, Failures=n-x,
 SE=se, Margin=margin, Lower=ci[1], Upper=ci[2]),digits=5)




Estimate
Successes
Failures
SE
Margin
Lower
Upper




0.44
396
504
0.01655
0.03243
0.40757
0.47243





Both counts (396 and 504) are comfortably above 10. The interval is approximately 0.4076 to 0.4724, or 40.76% to 47.24%. The margin is about 3.24 percentage points, not 3.24% of the estimated proportion.
If there are very few successes or failures, the Wald approximation may fail badly, including zero width or endpoints outside [0,1]. Do not silently clip endpoints and claim that coverage is repaired. Score or exact binomial methods are possible extensions. R’s default prop.test() uses a score-based approach with a continuity correction, so its interval need not equal this textbook Wald calculation.

title: Module 4: Proportions and Sample-size Planning
text:
Plan a proportion sample size
Before collecting new data, choose confidence, desired margin \(E\), and a planning value \(p^*\):
\[n=\left\lceil\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}^2p^*(1-p^*)}{E^2}\right\rceil.\]
The ceiling rounds up because the minimum required size must be met. A prior survey can suggest \(p^*\) but cannot guarantee the new population share. If no defensible value is available, \(.50\) maximizes \(p^*(1-p^*)\) and is conservative within this simple-sampling normal approximation.

# qnorm(): returns a normal lower-tail quantile; sd is standard deviation, not variance.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# ceiling() rounds upward to a whole number of completed responses; E=.025 means 2.5 percentage points.
# Compare the prior-survey planning share with .50; exact R quantiles may differ slightly from rounded tables.
z <- qnorm(.975)
E <- .025
planning_p <- c(.44,.50)
required <- ceiling(z^2*planning_p*(1-planning_p)/E^2)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Planning_share=planning_p, Completed_responses=required))




Planning_share
Completed_responses




0.44
1515


0.50
1537





The required completed samples are 1,515 using .44 and 1,537 using .50, matching the book’s recommendations. This controls the planned normal-approximation margin under the design assumptions. It does not guarantee response or remove coverage bias. Invitations must exceed completed responses if some invitees do not respond; nonresponse adjustment requires a justified response-rate assumption.

title: Module 4: Proportions and Sample-size Planning
text:
Plan precision for a mean
With a defensible planning SD \(\sigma^*\), the normal-based planning formula is
\[n=\left\lceil\left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}\sigma^*}{E}\right)^2\right\rceil.\]
Use \(E\) and \(\sigma^*\) in the same measurement units. A pilot or relevant historical source may provide the planning SD. This is a planning approximation when SD is estimated; a final unknown-SD mean interval still uses t. Complex designs and substantial sampling fractions need their corresponding design calculations.
For an original planning extension of the checked Lloyd’s example, take its $20 SD and request a $2 margin at 95% confidence:

# qnorm(): returns a normal lower-tail quantile; sd is standard deviation, not variance.
# Use the checked Lloyd's SD in an explicitly new planning question, not a new observed sample.
# Squaring gives required n; ceiling() preserves the requested maximum planned margin.
ceiling((qnorm(.975)*20/2)^2)

[1] 385


This gives 385 completed observations under the stated assumptions. Halving \(E\) roughly quadruples the required sample size. More precision has a cost; select a practically useful margin before collecting data.

title: Module 4: Sampling Distributions and Standard Errors
text:
Business case: repeated EAI samples
Return to the textbook’s 2,500 EAI employees, whose annual salaries have mean $71,800 and population SD $4,000; 60% completed management training. Compare repeated simple random samples of 30 employees. How variable are sample mean salary and sample training proportion? These are stated population summaries, not verified individual records.

نعود إلى مجتمع 2,500 موظف لدى EAI في الكتاب، حيث متوسط الراتب السنوي 71,800 دولار والانحراف المعياري للمجتمع 4,000 دولار، وقد أكمل 60% التدريب الإداري. نقارن عينات عشوائية بسيطة متكررة، حجم كل منها 30 موظفًا. ما مقدار تباين متوسط الراتب ونسبة إكمال التدريب بين العينات؟ هذه ملخصات المجتمع المعطاة، وليست سجلات فردية جرى التحقق منها.

title: Module 4: Sampling Distributions and Standard Errors
text:
Three different distributions
The population distribution describes individual salaries; a sample distribution describes the observed salaries in one sample; the sampling distribution describes one statistic over repeated samples. Their horizontal axes may share units, but their spreads answer different questions.
For independent, identically distributed observations with finite variance:
\[E(\bar X)=\mu,\qquad SE(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.\]
The population SD describes variability of individual values. The standard error is the SD of an estimator’s sampling distribution. When \(\sigma\) is unknown, \(s/\sqrt n\) estimates the SE; it does not become a known population quantity.
For independent binary observations with common probability \(p\):
\[E(\hat p)=p,\qquad SE(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}n}.\]
For simple random sampling without replacement from a finite population of size \(N\), multiply these SEs by \(\sqrt{(N-n)/(N-1)}\) when population variance uses denominator \(N\). Without-replacement observations are dependent. The textbook neglects this correction when \(n/N\leq .05\); this is an approximation, not exact independence.

# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# Compare the book's large-population approximation with the finite-population SE.
# sqrt() takes a square root; the correction uses N-1 because population variance uses denominator N.
N <- 2500
n <- 30
fpc <- sqrt((N - n)/(N - 1))
knitr::kable(data.frame(Statistic = c("Mean salary (USD/year)", "Training proportion"),
 Approximate_SE = c(4000/sqrt(n), sqrt(.6*.4/n)),
 Corrected_SE = fpc * c(4000/sqrt(n), sqrt(.6*.4/n))), digits = 5)




Statistic
Approximate_SE
Corrected_SE




Mean salary (USD/year)
730.29674
726.04696


Training proportion
0.08944
0.08892





The uncorrected salary SE is about $730.30, much smaller than the $4,000 individual SD. Multiplying sample size by four halves the uncorrected SE. Bias is not in this formula; smaller SE does not establish accuracy under a faulty design.

title: Module 4: Sampling Distributions and Standard Errors
section: Shape and the central limit theorem
text:
Shape and the central limit theorem
For independent normal observations, the sample mean is exactly normal for any \(n\). For many nonnormal populations with finite variance and appropriate independence, the central limit theorem makes the mean approximately normal as \(n\) grows. It does not make the raw observations normal. There is no universal sample size of 30 that handles arbitrary skewness, outliers, or dependence.
For a proportion, assess expected success and failure counts before a normal approximation. We use \(np\geq10\) and \(n(1-p)\geq10\) as a cautious teaching rule; this is a guideline, not a proof. Use estimated counts when constructing an interval with unknown \(p\).

title: Module 4: Sampling Distributions and Standard Errors
text:
An explicitly artificial illustration
The next simulation uses independent normal salaries with EAI’s stated mean and SD. It is an original model illustration: no claim is made that the finite EAI salary population is normal or that these are its actual employees. We deliberately omit finite population correction because this simulation draws from an independent model.

# mean(): computes an average; logical TRUE/FALSE values contribute 1/0, giving a proportion.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# sd(): computes sample standard deviation using denominator n-1.
# sqrt(): returns the nonnegative square root of a nonnegative number.
# replicate(B, expression) repeats a calculation B times; each result here is a new sample mean.
# rnorm(n, mean, sd) draws n artificial normal values using SD, not variance; set.seed() fixes the draw sequence.
set.seed(307312)
means <- replicate(4000, mean(rnorm(30, mean = 71800, sd = 4000)))
c(simulated_mean = mean(means), simulated_SE = sd(means), model_SE = 4000/sqrt(30))

simulated_mean   simulated_SE       model_SE 
    71783.2911       730.5734       730.2967 



# hist() displays the simulated sample means; breaks=30 requests roughly 30 histogram classes.
# abline(v=...) adds a vertical reference at the model's population mean.
hist(means, breaks = 30, col = "#B6D3E1", border = "white",
 main = "Artificial normal-model sample means (n = 30)", xlab = "Sample mean annual salary (USD)")
abline(v = 71800, col = "#356B8C", lwd = 2)








Original R simulation from a stated normal model; bars represent sample means, not individual employees.

title: Module 4: Sampling Distributions and Standard Errors
text:
Interpret a probability
Under that normal model, the chance a sample mean of 30 lies within $500 of $71,800 is:

# sqrt(): returns the nonnegative square root of a nonnegative number.
# pnorm() returns a normal lower-tail probability; subtract the two CDF values for an interval.
# sd receives the SE of a mean, not the $4,000 SD of individual salaries.
se <- 4000 / sqrt(30)
pnorm(72300, mean = 71800, sd = se) - pnorm(71300, mean = 71800, sd = se)

[1] 0.5064372


This is a probability about a future sample mean under the model. It is not a probability that one employee earns within $500 of the mean.

title: Module 3: Probability and Distributions
text:
Module 2 described recorded data. This module defines uncertainty about a selection or future outcome, then calculates probabilities under explicit models. Finish the descriptive-statistics review first.

Probability rules: outcomes, events, complements, intersections, and unions.
Conditional probability: reference groups, independence, multiplication, and Bayes’ theorem.
Discrete random variables: a probability mass function, cumulative probabilities, expected value, and variance.
Binomial and Poisson models: assumptions, count probabilities, exposure, and simulation.
Continuous distributions: uniform areas, normal tails, standardization, and quantiles.

title: Module 3: Binomial and Poisson Models — Practice

1. Select the model
Explain why the store example can be binomial with \(n=3\) and \(p=0.30\), and why the arrival count can be Poisson with mean 10 per 15 minutes. Give one plausible way each model’s assumptions could fail.

title: Module 3: Binomial and Poisson Models — Practice
text:
2. Translate binomial events
Calculate the probability of exactly two, at most two, at least two, and more than two purchases. Then find the expected count, variance, and SD. Explain the difference between dbinom() and pbinom() and the boundary needed for “at least two.”

title: Module 3: Binomial and Poisson Models — Practice
text:
3. Change the exposure
For the same stated arrival rate, find:

The mean count in three minutes.
The probability of no arrivals in three minutes.
The probability of at least two arrivals in three minutes.
The probability of more than ten arrivals in fifteen minutes.

Explain why the model mean must be tied to the interval and why the count has no fixed upper bound in the Poisson model.

title: Module 3: Binomial and Poisson Models — Practice
text:
4. Simulate and interpret
Use a fixed seed and simulate 10,000 three-customer binomial counts. Estimate the probability of at least two purchases and compare it with the exact value. Explain why a different seed may change the estimate and why this comparison does not establish model fit for real customers.

title: Module 3: Binomial and Poisson Models — Practice
text:
5. Sampling without replacement
Explain why taking three records from a finite list without replacement need not give independent trials with the same success probability. Do not apply a binomial model merely because there are three selections and two possible labels.
Submit a method-and-event table with results and a short interpretation. Return to the lesson.

title: Module 3: Binomial and Poisson Models
section: Business case: Martin Clothing Store purchases
text:
Business case: Martin Clothing Store purchases
At Martin Clothing Store, the book asks about the next three customers. The stated probability that a customer purchases is 0.30. Assume that probability is the same for each customer and that the three purchase decisions are independent. What is the probability that exactly two customers purchase? Each trial concerns one customer; the random variable counts purchases among the three customers.

في متجر Martin Clothing Store، يتناول سؤال الكتاب الزبائن الثلاثة القادمين. احتمال أن يشتري الزبون هو 0.30 وفق المعطيات. نفترض ثبات هذا الاحتمال لكل زبون واستقلال قرارات الشراء الثلاثة. ما احتمال أن يشتري زبونان بالضبط؟ تتعلق كل محاولة بزبون واحد، ويعدّ المتغير العشوائي المشترين بين الزبائن الثلاثة.

title: Module 3: Binomial and Poisson Models
text:
Check the binomial assumptions
Let \(X\) count purchases. A binomial model requires:

A fixed number of trials, \(n=3\).
Two outcomes on each trial: purchase or no purchase.
The same success probability on every trial, \(p=0.30\).
Independent trial outcomes.

“Success” is a mathematical label for the outcome being counted. It need not mean a desirable outcome in other applications. A shopping group making a joint purchase decision, or a promotion that changes during observation, could violate these assumptions.
We write \(X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\), with
\[P(X=x)=\binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x},\qquad x=0,1,\ldots,n.\]
Exactly two purchases can occur in three arrangements: purchase–purchase–no purchase, purchase–no purchase–purchase, or no purchase–purchase–purchase. Each arrangement has probability \(0.3^2(0.7)\), so the total is \(3(0.3^2)(0.7)=0.189\).

# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
# abs(): returns absolute values; a small tolerance in an equality check permits floating-point rounding.
# dbinom(x, size, prob) returns P(X=x); choose(3,2) counts arrangements of two successes.
# size is the fixed number of customers, while prob is the probability for one customer.
binomial <- data.frame(Purchases = 0:3, Probability = dbinom(0:3, size = 3, prob = 0.30))
kable(binomial, digits = 3)




Purchases
Probability

stopifnot(abs(dbinom(2, 3, .30) - choose(3, 2) * .30^2 * .70) < 1e-12)


Exact, cumulative, and upper-tail probabilities

# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# dbinom(): returns binomial point probabilities for size trials and success probability prob.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# names(): reads or assigns names to vector elements or table columns.
# unname(): removes names or dimension names without changing the underlying values.
# pbinom(k,...) gives P(X<=k); lower.tail=FALSE instead gives P(X>k).
# At least two means X>1, so its upper-tail call uses 1 rather than 2.
answers <- c("Exactly two" = dbinom(2, size = 3, prob = .30),
             "At most two" = pbinom(2, size = 3, prob = .30),
             "At least two" = pbinom(1, size = 3, prob = .30, lower.tail = FALSE),
             "At least one" = pbinom(0, size = 3, prob = .30, lower.tail = FALSE))
kable(data.frame(Event = names(answers), Probability = unname(answers)), digits = 3)




Event

The probability of exactly two purchases is 0.189; at least two has probability 0.216. Using pbinom(2, ..., lower.tail=FALSE) would calculate more than two, which is a different event.
For a binomial count,
\[E(X)=np=0.9,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=0.63.\]
The SD is \(\sqrt{0.63}\approx0.794\) purchases. The expected count 0.9 is an average across repetitions, not the purchase probability for a single customer and not a possible count for one three-customer group.

# The four bars exhaust this binomial distribution; their masses sum to one.
# Highlighting exactly two matches the business question rather than implying observed frequencies.

  geom_col(width = .65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", Probability)), vjust = -.4) +

section: Simulation checks an implication of the model
text:
Simulation checks an implication of the model

# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# dbinom(): returns binomial point probabilities for size trials and success probability prob.
# set.seed() makes the simulated illustration repeatable; rbinom() generates counts under the model.
# mean(simulated == 2) estimates the event probability, not the real store's unknown purchase rate.
set.seed(307312)
simulated <- rbinom(10000, size = 3, prob = .30)
kable(data.frame(Method = c("Exact model", "10,000 simulated groups"),
                 Probability_of_two = c(dbinom(2, 3, .30), mean(simulated == 2))), digits = 4)




Method
Probability_of_two




Exact model
0.1890

The simulated proportion should be near 0.189 but need not equal it. More repetitions usually reduce simulation variability. Agreement with a simulation generated from the same assumptions does not validate those assumptions for real customers.

title: Module 3: Binomial and Poisson Models
section: Business case: arrivals in an interval
text:
Business case: arrivals in an interval
The book considers arrivals at a large hospital emergency room on weekday mornings, with an average of 10 patients per 15-minute interval. Treat the example as a count-model exercise: assume a constant arrival rate, independent counts in disjoint intervals, and individual arrivals rather than batches. What is the probability of exactly five arrivals in 15 minutes, or exactly one arrival in three minutes? The counted event is one patient arrival; the exposure is a specified time interval. These stated inputs do not establish a current operational forecast.

يتناول الكتاب وصول المرضى إلى قسم الطوارئ في مستشفى كبير صباح أيام العمل، بمتوسط عشرة مرضى خلال كل فترة مدتها خمس عشرة دقيقة. نستخدم المثال للتدرّب على نموذج العدّ: نفترض ثبات معدل الوصول واستقلال الأعداد في الفترات غير المتداخلة، ووصول الأفراد دون دفعات جماعية. ما احتمال وصول خمسة مرضى بالضبط خلال خمس عشرة دقيقة، أو مريض واحد بالضبط خلال ثلاث دقائق؟ الحدث المعدود هو وصول مريض واحد، ومدة التعرّض هي الفترة الزمنية المحددة. لا تثبت هذه المعطيات توقعًا تشغيليًا حاليًا.

title: Module 3: Binomial and Poisson Models
section: The Poisson model uses an interval mean
text:
The Poisson model uses an interval mean
For a homogeneous Poisson process, a constant rate, independent increments, and negligible probability of multiple arrivals in a sufficiently short interval imply Poisson counts. Merely having a count variable or knowing its mean is insufficient.
If \(X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\),
\[P(X=x)=\frac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!},\qquad x=0,1,2,\ldots,\]
and \(E(X)=\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda\). Here, \(\lambda\) is the mean count for the specified interval. The book writes this mean as \(\mu\); R calls the argument lambda.
For 15 minutes, \(\lambda=10\). For three minutes at the same rate,
\[\lambda_{3\text{ min}}=10\times\frac{3}{15}=2.\]

# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# names(): reads or assigns names to vector elements or table columns.
# unname(): removes names or dimension names without changing the underlying values.
# dpois() returns an exact-count mass; ppois(k, lower.tail=FALSE) returns P(X>k).
# Scale lambda with the interval length before calculating a three-minute probability.
lambda_15 <- 10
lambda_3 <- lambda_15 * 3 / 15
poisson_answers <- c("Exactly 5 in 15 minutes" = dpois(5, lambda = lambda_15),
                     "More than 10 in 15 minutes" = ppois(10, lambda = lambda_15, lower.tail = FALSE),
                     "Exactly 1 in 3 minutes" = dpois(1, lambda = lambda_3))
kable(data.frame(Event = names(poisson_answers), Probability = unname(poisson_answers)), digits = 4)

Probability

More than 10 in 15 minutes
0.4170

The exact-five probability is about 0.0378. The exact-one probability over three minutes is about 0.2707. Keeping lambda=10 for three minutes would use the wrong exposure.

# dpois(): returns Poisson count probabilities; lambda is the mean for the stated exposure.
# ggplot(): starts a plot from data; additional layers are joined with +.

# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# labs(): sets axis titles, legend titles, plot titles, and captions.
# Plot a finite window of an infinite-support distribution; the omitted upper tail is not zero.
# The dashed line marks the model mean, while the highlighted bar marks exactly five arrivals.
poisson <- data.frame(Arrivals = 0:25, Probability = dpois(0:25, lambda = 10))
ggplot(poisson, aes(Arrivals, Probability, fill = Arrivals == 5)) +
  geom_col(width = .75) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed", color = "#56616D") +

  labs(x = "Arrivals in 15 minutes", y = "Probability mass",
       title = "Poisson model: mean count 10 per 15 minutes")

title: Module 3: Conditional Probability
section: Business case: the same restaurants, a new condition
text:
Business case: the same restaurants, a new condition
One record is selected uniformly from the 300 historical Los Angeles restaurants. The analyst now learns that its meal price is from USD 20 up to but not including USD 30. Among records meeting this condition, what is the probability of a Very Good rating? How does that answer differ from asking for the price band among Very Good restaurants?

يُختار سجل واحد باحتمالات متساوية من بيانات ثلاثمئة مطعم تاريخي في لوس أنجلوس. يعرف المحلّل الآن أن سعر الوجبة في المطعم المختار من 20 دولارًا إلى أقل من 30 دولارًا أمريكيًا. داخل السجلات التي تحقق هذا الشرط، ما احتمال أن يكون التقييم Very Good؟ وكيف تختلف الإجابة عن احتمال الانتماء إلى الفئة السعرية نفسها بين المطاعم ذات التقييم Very Good؟


# library(): loads a package so its functions can be used in this session.
# read.csv(): reads a comma-separated file into a data frame; its first row supplies column names by default.
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
# length(): counts elements in a vector or list.
# sum(): adds vector entries; on logical values it counts TRUE entries.
# theme_set(): sets the default theme for subsequent ggplot charts in this R session.
# theme_minimal(): uses a minimal chart style; base_size controls the base text size in points.
# Recreate the same events so conditioning changes the reference group rather than the data.
# mean(A[B]) averages A only within records satisfying B; this requires at least one B record.
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
r <- read.csv("data/module02/restaurant_ratings.csv")
A <- r$quality_rating == "Very Good"
B <- r$meal_price_usd >= 20 & r$meal_price_usd < 30
stopifnot(length(A) == 300, sum(B) == 118, sum(A) == 150, sum(A & B) == 64)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

title: Module 3: Conditional Probability
section: Conditional probability uses a restricted denominator
text:
Conditional probability uses a restricted denominator
For \(P(B)>0\),
\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.\]
The bar means given. It restricts the reference group to \(B\). For our selection, 64 restaurants satisfy both conditions, while 118 satisfy the known price condition:
\[P(A\mid B)=\frac{64/300}{118/300}=\frac{64}{118}\approx0.5424.\]
Reversing the condition changes the denominator:
\[P(B\mid A)=\frac{64}{150}\approx0.4267.\]

# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# rep(): repeats values; times repeats a vector and each repeats individual elements.
# sum(): adds vector entries; on logical values it counts TRUE entries.
# nrow(): returns the number of rows in a table or matrix.
# The numerator counts the same intersection, but each denominator matches its condition.
# kable() reports both directions and the joint probability to make the distinction visible.
comparison <- data.frame(Question = c("A and B", "A given B", "B given A"),
                         Numerator = rep(sum(A & B), 3),
                         Denominator = c(nrow(r), sum(B), sum(A)))
comparison$Probability <- comparison$Numerator / comparison$Denominator
kable(comparison, digits = 4)

Numerator
Denominator
Probability

Interpretation: 54.24% of restaurants in that price band are Very Good; 42.67% of Very Good restaurants are in that band. Neither is the 21.33% share of all records that satisfy both conditions. If \(P(B)=0\), this elementary conditional probability is undefined; do not divide by zero.

title: Module 3: Conditional Probability
text:
Multiplication and independence
Rearranging the conditional formula gives the general multiplication rule:
\[P(A\cap B)=P(B)P(A\mid B).\]
Events are independent when \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\). If \(P(B)>0\), this is equivalent to \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)\): knowing \(B\) leaves the probability of \(A\) unchanged.

# mean(): computes an average; logical TRUE/FALSE values contribute 1/0, giving a proportion.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# isTRUE(): returns TRUE only for a single nonmissing logical TRUE.
# Compare the actual joint probability with the product required by independence.
# all.equal() allows numerical tolerance; it does not perform a population hypothesis test.
joint <- mean(A & B)
product_if_independent <- mean(A) * mean(B)
kable(data.frame(Quantity = c("Actual P(A and B)", "P(A) times P(B)"),
                 Probability = c(joint, product_if_independent)), digits = 4)




Quantity
Probability




Actual P(A and B)
0.2133


P(A) times P(B)
0.1967




isTRUE(all.equal(joint, product_if_independent))

[1] FALSE


These events are dependent for uniform selection from these 300 records. That statement is an arithmetic property of the specified finite experiment, not an inferential test about a wider population.






NoteIndependent and mutually exclusive mean different things



Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together. Independent events leave each other’s probability unchanged. If two mutually exclusive events both have positive probability, they cannot be independent: their joint probability is zero, while the product of their probabilities is positive.



Selection without replacement
Suppose two records are selected successively and the first is not returned. If the first is Very Good, only 149 Very Good records among 299 remaining records are available for the second selection. Thus,
\[P(\text{both Very Good})=\frac{150}{300}\frac{149}{299}.\]
With replacement and independent selections, the corresponding probability is \((150/300)^2\). The mechanism determines whether the same probability can be multiplied twice.

title: Module 3: Conditional Probability
section: Business case: which supplier produced a bad part?
text:
Business case: which supplier produced a bad part?
In the book’s manufacturing example, 65% of parts come from supplier 1 and 35% from supplier 2. The stated bad-part probabilities are 2% for supplier 1 and 5% for supplier 2. One purchased part is selected at random and found to be bad. What is the probability that it came from supplier 2? One outcome concerns one part; these are the textbook’s probability inputs, not newly collected inspection observations.

في مثال التصنيع في الكتاب، يأتي 65% من القطع من المورّد الأول و35% من المورّد الثاني. واحتمال أن تكون القطعة معيبة هو 2% لدى المورّد الأول و5% لدى المورّد الثاني. تُختار قطعة مشتراة عشوائيًا ويتبيّن أنها معيبة. ما احتمال أن تكون من المورّد الثاني؟ تتعلق النتيجة بقطعة واحدة؛ وهذه احتمالات معطاة في الكتاب، وليست مشاهدات فحص جُمعت حديثًا.

title: Module 3: Conditional Probability
text:
Total probability and Bayes’ theorem
Let \(S_1,S_2\) denote the two suppliers and \(D\) a bad part. The suppliers are mutually exclusive and cover all parts. Multiply along each supplier-and-condition path, then add the disjoint bad-part paths:
\[P(D)=P(S_1)P(D\mid S_1)+P(S_2)P(D\mid S_2).\]
Bayes’ theorem restricts those paths to the ones consistent with the new information:
\[P(S_2\mid D)=\frac{P(S_2)P(D\mid S_2)}{P(D)}.\]

# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# sum(): adds vector entries; on logical values it counts TRUE entries.
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
# abs(): returns absolute values; a small tolerance in an equality check permits floating-point rounding.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# These priors and bad-part rates are stated model inputs from textbook p.201, not raw data.
# Multiply within each supplier path, then divide by the total bad-part probability.
suppliers <- data.frame(Supplier = c("Supplier 1", "Supplier 2"),
                        Prior = c(0.65, 0.35), Bad_given_supplier = c(0.02, 0.05))
suppliers$Joint_bad <- suppliers$Prior * suppliers$Bad_given_supplier
p_bad <- sum(suppliers$Joint_bad)
suppliers$Supplier_given_bad <- suppliers$Joint_bad / p_bad
stopifnot(abs(p_bad - 0.0305) < 1e-12,
          abs(sum(suppliers$Supplier_given_bad) - 1) < 1e-12)
kable(suppliers, digits = 4)




Supplier
Prior
Bad_given_supplier
Joint_bad
Supplier_given_bad




Supplier 1
0.65
0.02

0.4262


Supplier 2
0.35

The probability of a bad part is 0.0305. Among bad parts, supplier 2 accounts for \(0.0175/0.0305\approx0.5738\), or 57.38%. This reverses \(P(D\mid S_2)=0.05\); the two conditional probabilities answer different questions. Supplier 2 has a smaller prior share but a higher stated bad-part rate.

# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# rep(): repeats values; times repeats a vector and each repeats individual elements.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# ggplot(): starts a plot from data; additional layers are joined with +.
# aes(): maps variables to visual properties such as x, y, fill, color, or group.
# geom_col(): draws bars at supplied heights; it does not count records.
# position_dodge(): places groups side by side; width controls their horizontal separation.
# geom_text(): draws labels from mapped data; position and hjust/vjust control placement.
# sprintf(): formats text using placeholders such as %.2f for two decimal places.
# scale_fill_manual(): assigns explicit fill colors to categories; named values preserve category-color mappings.
# scale_y_continuous(): controls numeric y-axis breaks, labels, limits, and spacing.
# paste0(): joins text with no separator; collapse can combine a vector into one string.
# labs(): sets axis titles, legend titles, plot titles, and captions.
# theme(): customizes non-data plot elements such as legends, grids, and axis text.
# Compare supplier shares before inspection with shares conditional on a bad part.
# Fixed y limits and direct labels keep the prior/posterior comparison on the same scale.
plot_data <- data.frame(Supplier = rep(suppliers$Supplier, 2),
                       Information = rep(c("Before inspection", "Given a bad part"), each = 2),
                       Probability = c(suppliers$Prior, suppliers$Supplier_given_bad))
ggplot(plot_data, aes(Supplier, Probability, fill = Information)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * Probability)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#B6D3E1", "#E4B47E")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.8), labels = function(x) paste0(100 * x, "%")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Supplier probability", fill = NULL,
       title = "Evidence changes the reference group") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Original R chart calculated from the book’s two-supplier probability inputs, Table 4.6 and accompanying text, p.201.

title: Module 3: Conditional Probability

A calculation sequence to remember

Identify the event and the information being conditioned on.
Write the relevant joint paths and multiply their probabilities.
Add disjoint paths to obtain the denominator.
Divide the relevant joint probability by that denominator.
Interpret the result in the restricted group and state the input assumptions.

title: Module 2: Numerical Measures — Practice
text:
1. Describe the center

Calculate the number of audits, total recorded duration, mean, and median.
Show which sorted positions determine the median.
Identify the statistical mode using value frequencies. Explain why mode(x) does not answer that question in R.
Write a sentence explaining the mean and median to an audit manager. Explain why neither number guarantees a future completion date.

title: Module 2: Numerical Measures — Practice
text:
2. Quantify variability

Calculate minimum, maximum, and range.
Calculate the sum of squared deviations from the sample mean, then divide by n - 1 to obtain the sample variance. Check against var(x).
Take its square root and check against sd(x).
Give the units of the range, variance, and standard deviation.
Explain why dividing by n would produce a different descriptive quantity and why having all 20 CSV rows does not automatically make them the full population of interest.

title: Module 2: Numerical Measures — Practice
text:
3. Quartiles and a boxplot

Calculate \(Q_1\), median, and \(Q_3\) with quantile(x, c(.25,.5,.75), type = 6).
Calculate IQR and the five-number summary.
Calculate both 1.5-IQR fences and identify any flagged values.
Identify the actual whisker endpoints. Explain how they differ from the fences and the overall maximum.
Draw a boxplot with those quartiles and whiskers. Label its units and state the convention. If using a software default, check that its quartiles match your stated method for these data.
State what you would investigate before deciding whether a flagged observation is erroneous.

title: Module 2: Numerical Measures — Practice
text:
4. Sensitivity and relative measures

Replace only the largest audit duration with 60 days in a separate copy.
Compare mean, median, sample SD, range, and IQR before and after the hypothetical change.
Explain which measures changed most and why. Do not treat the hypothetical dataset as a corrected source file.
Calculate the CV for the original audits and interpret it.
Calculate the sample z-score of the original 33-day audit. Explain why it may be flagged by the IQR rule while having a z-score smaller than 3.
Explain why a CV for Celsius temperature is not meaningful in the same way as a CV for elapsed duration.

title: Module 2: Numerical Measures — Practice
text:
5. Return to the restaurant question
For each quality category, calculate group size, mean, median, sample SD, \(Q_1\), \(Q_3\), and IQR. Preserve the order Good, Very Good, Excellent.

Which group has the highest median price? Which has the smallest IQR?
Calculate the difference between the Excellent and Good median prices, in USD. Describe it as a difference in group medians, not as an individual restaurant’s price change.
Compare the groups with side-by-side boxplots, using the same quartile convention as the table.
Write a short interpretation of center, spread, and overlap. Explain why these data do not prove that changing a rating causes the price to change.

section: 6. Explain the limitations of a summary

6. Explain the limitations of a summary
Use the teaching-comparisons CSV, separate from the textbook bundle.

For the seven dollar values (example == "extreme_value"), calculate the mean and median. Which better describes the middle of the observations? When would the mean still be useful? Explain what information is lost when these seven observations are compressed into a single mean. Does the mode answer the same question as the median?
For S1–S5 (example == "same_mean"), verify that every mean is 200 and calculate each range. Explain what the mean alone conceals.
For A and B (example == "same_range"), calculate mean, range, mean absolute deviation about the mean, and sample SD. Explain how two sets with identical means and ranges can differ internally.
For the seven dollar amounts, calculate the range and explain why USD 99 does not describe the spread of most amounts. If only USD 100 became USD 1000 in a hypothetical copy, what would the range be? What would remain unchanged about the other six amounts?
Explain why replacing range with SD does not remove sensitivity to extreme values. What additional information do median, IQR, and a plot provide?

title: Module 2: Relationships Between Variables
text:
Lessons 1–3 describe variables individually and compare numerical distributions across groups. We now ask how two variables relate within the same observations.

title: Module 2: Relationships Between Variables
section: Business case: quality ratings and meal-price bands
text:
Business case: quality ratings and meal-price bands
An analyst studies 300 Los Angeles restaurants from the book’s historical teaching dataset. Each restaurant has an ordered quality rating and a meal price in US dollars. The analyst asks: Within each quality category, how are restaurants distributed across price bands? A second question reverses the conditioning: Within a price band, how are quality ratings distributed? These questions use the same records but different denominators.

يدرس محلّل بيانات ثلاثمئة مطعم في لوس أنجلوس من بيانات الكتاب التعليمية التاريخية. لكل مطعم تقييم جودة مرتب وسعر وجبة بالدولار الأمريكي. يسأل المحلّل: داخل كل فئة من فئات الجودة، كيف تتوزع المطاعم على فئات الأسعار؟ ثم يعكس السؤال: داخل فئة سعرية محددة، كيف تتوزع تقييمات الجودة؟ يستخدم السؤالان السجلات نفسها، لكن مقام حساب النسبة يختلف بينهما.

Download Restaurant CSV. One row is one restaurant. The four bands are [10,20), [20,30), [30,40), [40,50) USD: include the lower boundary and exclude the upper one. A price of USD 20 belongs to the second band. For these whole-dollar observations, these correspond to the book’s USD 10–19, 20–29, 30–39, and 40–49 classes.

Show R code
# factor(): stores categorical values; levels fixes their permitted order and labels can rename their display.
# ifelse(): chooses a value element by element according to a logical condition.
# sprintf(): formats text using placeholders such as %.2f for two decimal places.
# paste0(): joins text with no separator; collapse can combine a vector into one string.
# rowSums(): sums each row separately.
# ggplot(): starts a plot from data; additional layers are joined with +.
# aes(): maps variables to visual properties such as x, y, fill, color, or group.
# geom_col(): draws bars at supplied heights; it does not count records.
# geom_text(): draws labels from mapped data; position and hjust/vjust control placement.
# scale_fill_manual(): assigns explicit fill colors to categories; named values preserve category-color mappings.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# scale_x_discrete(): controls category order, labels, and spacing on the x-axis.
# scale_y_continuous(): controls numeric y-axis breaks, labels, limits, and spacing.
# seq(): creates an equally spaced sequence; by sets spacing and length.out sets the number of values.
# labs(): sets axis titles, legend titles, plot titles, and captions.
# theme(): customizes non-data plot elements such as legends, grids, and axis text.
# as.data.frame() reshapes the percentage table into one row per quality-price combination.
# position_stack() places segments and labels within each 100% quality-group bar.
bar_data <- as.data.frame(row_pct, responseName = "Percent")
bar_data$Quality <- factor(bar_data$Quality, levels = quality_levels)
bar_data$Price <- factor(bar_data$Price, levels = price_labels)
bar_data$Label <- ifelse(bar_data$Percent >= 8, sprintf("%.1f%%",bar_data$Percent), "")
quality_axis <- paste0(quality_levels, "\n(n = ", rowSums(counts), ")")
ggplot(bar_data, aes(Quality, Percent, fill = Price)) +
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE), width = .62,
           colour = "white", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Label), position = position_stack(vjust = .5, reverse = TRUE),
            colour = "#22313C", size = 3.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#DCE8EF", "#ACC9DA", "#E8CFA5", "#C9D8BD"), drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = quality_axis) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0,100,25), limits = c(0,100)) +
  labs(title = "Price distributions differ across quality categories",
       x = "Quality rating", y = "Within-group percentage", fill = "Meal price (USD)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Show R code
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
# abs(): returns absolute values; a small tolerance in an equality check permits floating-point rounding.
# Index counts and percentages by quality row and price-band column.
# stopifnot() stops execution if the count or either conditioning denominator is incorrect.
stopifnot(counts["Very Good",2] == 64,
          abs(row_pct["Very Good",2]-100*64/150) < 1e-10,
          abs(column_pct["Very Good",2]-100*64/118) < 1e-10)








NoteCalculate from counts, then round



Our percentages come directly from the checked counts. Round only for display. Independently rounded cells may not total exactly 100%. The book’s Table 2.11 prints some cells differently (for example 33.4% for 22/66); our calculated value rounds to 33.3%. We retain the observations and reproducible arithmetic.


Crosstabs show an association between quality and price bands here. They do not show that raising a price improves quality. Grouping boundaries can affect the display, and combining subgroups can hide or reverse patterns. The book develops this aggregation issue as Simpson’s paradox in §2.3. A full subgroup analysis would require relevant subgroup data, which this Restaurant file does not contain.

title: Module 2: Relationships Between Variables
section: Business case: commercials and weekly electronics sales
text:
Business case: commercials and weekly electronics sales
A San Francisco electronics store records 10 weeks of television-commercial counts and sales. One row pairs the commercials and sales from the same week. Sales are recorded in hundreds of US dollars: a value of 50 means USD 5,000. The question is: Do weeks with more commercials tend to have higher sales? These historical observations can describe an association, but they do not isolate the effect of advertising.

title: Module 2: Relationships Between Variables
text:
Scatterplots: inspect the paired pattern
A scatterplot places one numerical variable on each axis and one point for each paired observation. Keep each week’s pair together. Sorting the two columns independently destroys the observed relationship.


Show R code
# ggplot(): starts a plot from data; additional layers are joined with +.
# aes(): maps variables to visual properties such as x, y, fill, color, or group.
# scale_y_continuous(): controls numeric y-axis breaks, labels, limits, and spacing.
# expansion(): sets extra axis space; mult is relative padding and add is padding in axis units.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# labs(): sets axis titles, legend titles, plot titles, and captions.
# geom_point() draws each paired week; geom_text() labels points with week identifiers.
# nudge_y moves labels above points, and scale_x_continuous() sets the count-axis tick marks.
ggplot(electronics, aes(commercials, sales_hundreds_usd)) +
  geom_point(size = 3.2, colour = "#2878A5") +
  geom_text(aes(label = week), nudge_y = 1, size = 3.5, colour = "#56616D") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(.06,.12))) +
  labs(title = "More commercials accompany higher weekly sales",
       x = "Number of television commercials", y = "Weekly sales (hundreds of USD)")








Figure 2: Original R scatterplot of the ten checked Electronics observations. Labels identify weeks. No fitted regression model is required for this descriptive display.





Read four features before calculating a coefficient:

Direction: as commercials increase, sales tend to increase. This is a positive association.
Form: the pattern is approximately straight rather than clearly curved.
Strength: points cluster fairly closely around an upward linear pattern, with variation at each commercial count.
Unusual observations: look for isolated points and values far from the overall pattern. The plot alone cannot establish whether a record is erroneous.

The count is on the horizontal axis because it is the proposed explanatory variable for this question. That placement does not establish cause and effect. We leave connecting lines out because our immediate question concerns the paired relationship, rather than a chronological sales path.

title: Module 2: Relationships Between Variables
text:
Covariance: do deviations move together?
The sample covariance is
\[s_{xy}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{n-1}.\]
When both observations are above their means, or both below, their product of deviations is positive. Opposite signs give a negative product. Summing these products describes whether deviations tend to move together.


Show R code
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# mean(): computes an average; logical TRUE/FALSE values contribute 1/0, giving a proportion.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
# Subtract each sample mean and multiply the paired deviations week by week.
# sum() combines the cross-products; cov() divides their sum by n-1 for sample covariance.
x <- electronics$commercials
y <- electronics$sales_hundreds_usd
products <- data.frame(Week = electronics$week, x = x, y = y,
                       x_deviation = x-mean(x), y_deviation = y-mean(y),
                       Product = (x-mean(x))*(y-mean(y)))

Here \(\bar{x}=3\), \(\bar{y}=51\), and the sum of products is 99. Thus \(s_{xy}=99/9=11\), in commercials × hundreds of USD. Positive covariance agrees with the upward scatterplot.
Covariance depends on measurement units. Its sign helps describe direction, but its magnitude alone cannot establish that an association is strong. For a complete population, the population covariance uses population means and denominator \(N\). R’s cov() uses the sample denominator \(n-1\).

title: Module 2: Relationships Between Variables
text:
Correlation: standardize the linear association
The Pearson sample correlation divides covariance by the sample standard deviations:
\[r=\frac{s_{xy}}{s_xs_y}.\]
It requires paired numerical observations with nonzero variation in both variables. It is unitless, ranges from −1 to +1, and describes linear association:







Value
Meaning




\(r=+1\)
All points lie on a straight line with positive slope


\(r=-1\)
All points lie on a straight line with negative slope


\(r\) near zero
Little linear association; a nonlinear relationship may remain


Larger \(|r|\)
Stronger linear association, interpreted with the plot and context





Show R code
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
# abs(): returns absolute values; a small tolerance in an equality check permits floating-point rounding.
# cor() calculates Pearson linear correlation from the paired observations.
# Dividing cov(x,y) by sd(x)*sd(y) checks the same unitless calculation explicitly.
r <- cor(x,y)
kable(data.frame(Quantity = c("Sample SD: commercials", "Sample SD: sales (hundreds of USD)",
                              "Sample covariance", "Pearson correlation"),
                 Value = c(sd(x),sd(y),cov(x,y),r)), digits = 4)





Quantity

Show R code
stopifnot(abs(r-cov(x,y)/(sd(x)*sd(y))) < 1e-10,
          abs(r-0.9304906) < 1e-7)


Interpretation: across these ten weeks, commercials and sales have a strong positive linear association, \(r\approx0.9305\), consistent with the book’s rounded value 0.93. This does not mean “sales increase by 93%,” and correlation does not give a change in sales per additional commercial. Estimating such a change requires a model, developed later in regression.

Changing units: covariance changes, correlation stays


Show R code
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
# abs(): returns absolute values; a small tolerance in an equality check permits floating-point rounding.
# Multiply recorded sales by 100 to convert hundreds of USD into USD.
# cov() scales by the same factor; cor() is unchanged under this positive unit conversion.
y_usd <- 100*y
units <- data.frame(Sales_unit = c("Hundreds of USD", "USD"),
                    Sample_covariance = c(cov(x,y),cov(x,y_usd)),
                    Correlation = c(cor(x,y),cor(x,y_usd)))
kable(units, digits = 4)

          abs(cor(x,y_usd)-cor(x,y)) < 1e-10)


Converting sales to USD changes covariance from 11 to 1100, but the correlation stays 0.9305. The underlying relationship has not changed. Positive changes of measurement units and shifts of origin leave Pearson correlation unchanged. Correlation also treats \(x\) and \(y\) symmetrically: cor(x,y) equals cor(y,x).

title: Module 2: Relationships Between Variables
section: Why a correlation coefficient needs its plot
text:
Why a correlation coefficient needs its plot
The following are artificial teaching patterns, not Electronics data. The curved pattern uses \(y=x^2\) for \(x=-4,-3,\ldots,4\).


Show R code
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# factor(): stores categorical values; levels fixes their permitted order and labels can rename their display.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
# abs(): returns absolute values; a small tolerance in an equality check permits floating-point rounding.
# ggplot(): starts a plot from data; additional layers are joined with +.
# aes(): maps variables to visual properties such as x, y, fill, color, or group.
# geom_point(): draws a point for each row at its mapped x and y values.
# labs(): sets axis titles, legend titles, plot titles, and captions.
# rbind() combines three explicitly artificial paired patterns: y=x, y=-x, and y=x^2.
# facet_wrap() separates the plots; cor() verifies that a curve can have zero linear correlation.
u <- -4:4
patterns <- rbind(data.frame(Pattern = "Positive line: r = 1", x = u, y = u),
                  data.frame(Pattern = "Negative line: r = -1", x = u, y = -u),
                  data.frame(Pattern = "Curve: r = 0", x = u, y = u^2))
patterns$Pattern <- factor(patterns$Pattern,
  levels = c("Positive line: r = 1", "Negative line: r = -1", "Curve: r = 0"))
stopifnot(cor(u,u) == 1, cor(u,-u) == -1, abs(cor(u,u^2)) < 1e-10)
ggplot(patterns, aes(x,y)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "#2878A5") +
  facet_wrap(~Pattern, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Zero correlation can conceal a clear relationship",
       x = "x (arbitrary units)", y = "y (arbitrary units)")








Figure 3: Original artificial examples. Pearson correlation captures straight-line direction but can be zero despite a clear curved relationship. Panel axes use arbitrary units.





Keep these limitations in view:

Nonlinearity: \(r=0\) does not establish that variables are unrelated or independent.
Influential observations: an isolated observation can substantially change correlation. Investigate it and compare results transparently; preserve valid records.
Restricted range and mixed groups: a narrow observed range or a mixture of subgroups can change the apparent association. Inspect context and subgroup information when available.
Causation: seasonal demand, promotions, or other unmeasured factors might affect both advertising and sales. These are possible explanations to investigate, not recorded facts about this store.
Scope: ten observed weeks do not establish a stable relationship for all future weeks. Repeated weeks may also be dependent; calculation alone does not justify inferential claims.

Computing Pearson correlation requires no normality assumption by itself. Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals for association require additional assumptions and belong to later modules.

text:

title: Module 2: Frequency Tables and Charts
section: Business case: which soft drinks were purchased?
text:
Business case: which soft drinks were purchased?
A manager wants a clear description of the brands selected in 50 soft-drink purchases. Which brand was purchased most often, and what proportion of purchases did each brand represent? The book records purchases of five brands; one observation is one purchase, not necessarily one distinct customer.

يريد مدير أن يحصل على وصف واضح للعلامات التجارية المختارة في خمسين عملية شراء لمشروبات غازية. ما العلامة الأكثر شراءً، وما نسبة عمليات الشراء التي تمثلها كل علامة؟ يتضمن مثال الكتاب خمس علامات تجارية، وتمثل كل مشاهدة عملية شراء واحدة، وليس بالضرورة عميلًا مختلفًا.

Download the CSV. Use brand_book_label for the book’s category names. The CSV also preserves brand_original: Coke Classic is mapped to Coca-Cola and Pepsi-Cola to Pepsi. This is a documented label alignment, not a change to the counts.


Show R code
# read.csv() imports the teaching file as a data frame with named columns.
# The $ operator selects brand_book_label, the documented textbook-label column.
soft <- read.csv("data/module02/soft_drinks.csv")
# Use this column for the textbook's category labels:
soft$brand_book_label

title: Module 2: Frequency Tables and Charts
section: From observations to a frequency table
text:
From observations to a frequency table
A frequency is the number of observations assigned to a category or numerical class. A frequency distribution lists those categories or classes together with their counts.
For one categorical variable, each observation must belong to exactly one category. Check that categories are consistently named, missing values are handled explicitly, and no record is counted twice. An omitted category with zero observations can still be relevant to the question.
For a dataset of size \(n\) and a category frequency \(f\):
\[
\text{Relative frequency}=\frac{f}{n},\qquad
\text{Percentage}=100\frac{f}{n}.
\]
A relative frequency is a proportion, such as 0.38. Its percentage equivalent is 38%, not 0.38%.


Show R code
# names(): reads or assigns names to vector elements or table columns.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
# identical(): requires exact equality of values, types, and attributes.
# as.integer(): converts to integers by truncating numeric fractional parts; it does not round to nearest.
# sum(): adds vector entries; on logical values it counts TRUE entries.
# abs(): returns absolute values; a small tolerance in an equality check permits floating-point rounding.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# table() counts brand occurrences; as.data.frame() turns the counts into columns.
# Divide by nrow(soft) for proportions and multiply by 100 for percentages.
brand_table <- as.data.frame(table(soft$brand))
names(brand_table) <- c("Brand", "Frequency")
brand_table$Relative_frequency <- brand_table$Frequency / nrow(soft)
brand_table$Percent <- 100 * brand_table$Relative_frequency
stopifnot(identical(as.integer(brand_table$Frequency), c(19L, 8L, 5L, 13L, 5L)),
          sum(brand_table$Frequency) == 50,
          abs(sum(brand_table$Relative_frequency) - 1) < 1e-12)
kable(brand_table, digits = c(0, 0, 2, 0),
      col.names = c("Brand", "Frequency", "Relative frequency", "Percent (%)"))

Interpretation: Coca-Cola accounts for 19 of 50 purchases (38%), the largest observed share. This describes the sample of purchases; it does not establish a market share for all consumers or measure profit.

title: Module 2: Frequency Tables and Charts
text:
Bar charts: compare categories
A bar chart places categories on one axis and their counts or percentages on the other. The bars are separated because categories are distinct. The length of each bar communicates the quantity, so the quantitative axis should start at zero.
Nominal brands have no inherent ranking. Alphabetical order is reasonable for lookup; descending frequency makes a popularity comparison easier. For ordinal categories, retain their meaningful order rather than sorting them by frequency.


Show R code
# as.character(): converts values to character text; for a factor it returns displayed category labels.
# rev(): reverses the order of a vector.
# ggplot(): starts a plot from data; additional layers are joined with +.
# aes(): maps variables to visual properties such as x, y, fill, color, or group.
# scale_x_continuous(): controls numeric x-axis breaks, labels, limits, and spacing.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# seq(): creates an equally spaced sequence; by sets spacing and length.out sets the number of values.
# labs(): sets axis titles, legend titles, plot titles, and captions.
# order() ranks the frequency rows; factor() fixes the displayed category order.
# geom_col() plots the supplied counts and geom_text() places their labels.
ranked <- brand_table[order(-brand_table$Frequency, as.character(brand_table$Brand)), ]
ranked$Brand <- factor(ranked$Brand, levels = rev(as.character(ranked$Brand)))
ggplot(ranked, aes(Frequency, Brand)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2878A5", width = .65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Frequency), hjust = -.35) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 22), breaks = seq(0, 20, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Coca-Cola has the largest observed purchase count",
       x = "Purchases (out of 50)", y = NULL)








Figure 1: Original R chart from the checked SoftDrink CSV. Counts match book Table 2.2, printed p.38.





The same counts can be shown as percentages. Do not treat counts and percentages from this one sample as separate findings: one is a rescaling of the other.

Pie charts: show shares of one whole
A pie chart divides a circle into slices whose angles represent proportions of a whole. A 38% share has an angle of \(0.38\times360^\circ=136.8^\circ\).
Use it only when categories describe nonoverlapping parts of one clearly defined total. With many categories or similar shares, bars are easier to compare. Use a flat display and direct labels; 3D perspective can distort apparent slice sizes.


Show R code
# paste0(): joins text with no separator; collapse can combine a vector into one string.
# ggplot(): starts a plot from data; additional layers are joined with +.
# aes(): maps variables to visual properties such as x, y, fill, color, or group.
# geom_col(): draws bars at supplied heights; it does not count records.
# geom_text(): draws labels from mapped data; position and hjust/vjust control placement.
# scale_fill_manual(): assigns explicit fill colors to categories; named values preserve category-color mappings.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# theme_void(): removes axes and most non-data decoration.
# theme(): customizes non-data plot elements such as legends, grids, and axis text.
# coord_polar(theta = "y") turns the stacked percentage bar into a circle.
# position_stack(vjust = .5) centers each label within its corresponding slice.
pie_data <- brand_table
pie_data$label <- paste0(pie_data$Brand, "\n", pie_data$Percent, "%")
ggplot(pie_data, aes(x = "", y = Percent, fill = Brand)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, colour = "white") +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), position = position_stack(vjust = .5), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#99C1D9", "#D9E8F0", "#AAD5B7", "#F1DE99", "#E9B5B9")) +
  theme_void() + theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 2: Original R chart: the same 50 purchases shown as percentages of one whole. Colors distinguish categories; they do not encode a ranking.





Discussion: Which display makes the tie between Sprite and Dr. Pepper easier to assess? Which is easier to read when brand names are long?


Percentages need a denominator
Always name the whole: here it is 50 recorded purchases. If comparing datasets with different sample sizes, percentages can be more useful than raw counts, but differences in sampling and population coverage still matter.
Do not cumulatively add nominal categories as though they form a natural numerical progression. Adding the three most frequent brands can answer a stated “top three” question; the order is an analytical choice, not a property of the brand variable. Here the three largest shares total 80%.

title: Module 2: Frequency Tables and Charts
section: Business case: how long do audits take?
text:
Business case: how long do audits take?
An accounting firm wants to describe the completion times of 20 year-end audits, recorded in days. Which duration ranges occur most often, and how many audits finish before a chosen threshold? title: Module 2: Frequency Tables and Charts
text:
Group numerical values into classes
Grouping replaces individual values with ranges. It makes patterns easier to see, but loses detail: a grouped table does not tell us every exact value inside a range.
Choose a number of classes, a convenient width, and boundaries that cover all observations. For Audit, the smallest value is 12 and the largest is 33 days. With five classes, an initial width estimate is \((33-12)/5=4.2\) days. Following the book, use a convenient 5-day width, starting at 10 days.
Our intervals are [10,15), [15,20), [20,25), [25,30), [30,35). A square bracket includes the boundary; a round bracket excludes it. Thus, 15 belongs to [15,20), while 20 belongs to [20,25). For these whole-day records, these groups reproduce the book’s 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–29, and 30–34 classes.






NoteClass rules



Every value must fall into exactly one class. Avoid gaps, overlap, or an uncovered maximum. Retain empty classes when they are part of the chosen numerical scale. There is no universally best number of classes: check that your choice reveals rather than hides the distribution.




Show R code
# as.data.frame(): converts an object to a rectangular data frame.
# names(): reads or assigns names to vector elements or table columns.
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# nrow(): returns the number of rows in a table or matrix.
# stopifnot(): stops execution if any supplied condition is FALSE; successful checks produce no output.
# anyNA(): returns TRUE if any value is missing; !anyNA(...) requires no missing values.
# sum(): adds vector entries; on logical values it counts TRUE entries.
# identical(): requires exact equality of values, types, and attributes.
# as.integer(): converts to integers by truncating numeric fractional parts; it does not round to nearest.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# seq(10,35,5) sets class boundaries; cut() assigns each audit to an interval.
# right = FALSE gives [lower, upper) classes; table() counts each class.
boundaries <- seq(10, 35, 5)
audit$class <- cut(audit$audit_days, breaks = boundaries, right = FALSE)
audit_table <- as.data.frame(table(audit$class))
names(audit_table) <- c("Days", "Frequency")
audit_table$Relative_frequency <- audit_table$Frequency / nrow(audit)
audit_table$Percent <- 100 * audit_table$Relative_frequency
stopifnot(!anyNA(audit$class), sum(audit_table$Frequency) == 20,
          identical(as.integer(audit_table$Frequency), c(4L, 8L, 5L, 2L, 1L)))
kable(audit_table, digits = c(0, 0, 2, 0),
      col.names = c("Duration class (days)", "Frequency", "Relative frequency", "Percent (%)"))
